lesson.title: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
lesson.subtitle: From make to machen, cook to kochen, and book to Buch

hook.title: The Ghost in the Throat
hook.content: During the High German Consonant Shift, ancient Germanic voiceless stop 'k' softened into a breathy fricative written as 'ch'. While English kept the hard stop across the North Sea, German speakers moved the sound into the throat, turning make into machen and cook into kochen.

footnotes.title: Velar Spirantization
footnotes.content: Post-vocalic voiceless velar stop [k] relaxed into voiceless velar/palatal fricatives [x] and [ç]. One letter, two sounds, decided by the vowel before it.

pattern.title: Ach-Laut vs. Ich-Laut: The Vowel Compass
pattern.content: German 'ch' produces two distinct sounds dictated entirely by the preceding vowel. After back vowels (a, o, u), the tongue pulls back into the throat to produce the rough 'Ach-Laut' [x] (as in Scottish loch: machen, kochen, Buch). After front vowels (e, i, ä, ö, ü) or consonants (l, r), the tongue arches forward to whisper the soft 'Ich-Laut' [ç] (identical to the first sound in English 'huge' or 'human': sprechen, brechen, Milch, Küche). English even kept this soft shift in noun-verb pairs: seek vs. beseech, and speak vs. speech!

footnotes.title: Palatal vs. Velar
footnotes.content: Ach-Laut [x] follows back vowels; Ich-Laut [ç] follows front vowels and liquid consonants.

footnotes.title: Say What You Read
footnotes.content: German spells the way it sounds: each vowel letter holds one sound — the i of finden is short, like the i of English 'bit' — and the letter laws own the consonants, so every word you read tells you how to say it. When a cluster like the schl- of schlafen tangles on your tongue, slow down; the sounds sit together fine at half speed. And don't let regional accents shake you: you might hear a harder /ick/ in Berlin or an /ish/-tinged ich in the south — variants to recognize, never to learn.

pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “German ch is one sound.” It is two, and the vowel *before* it decides which: after a, o, u it is the Scots ch of loch (Buch, machen); after i, e and the consonants it is the soft h of “hue” (ich, Milch). One letter, two sounds, one rule.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German verb for 'to cook' using the K → CH shift (cook + en):
exercises.affirmation: You melted the k into ch and hung the -en — cook is kochen, audible in your throat now.
exercises.explanation: Stem 'koch-' (medial K shifted to CH after back vowel 'o') + infinitive suffix '-en' = kochen.

exercises.prompt: Match the English K words to their German CH cognates:
exercises.meaning: to seek, to speak, book, milk
exercises.affirmation: Four k-words melted on sight — the throat-sound is becoming a reflex.
exercises.explanation: Medial and final English K regularly shifts to German CH ([x] after back vowels, [ç] after front vowels and consonants).

exercises.prompt: Why does 'Buch' use the Ach-Laut ([x]), while 'Küche' uses the Ich-Laut ([ç])?
options: The sounds are completely interchangeable in German
Ach-Laut follows back vowels (u); Ich-Laut follows front vowels (ü)
Buch is neuter and Küche is feminine
exercises.target_answer: Ach-Laut follows back vowels (u); Ich-Laut follows front vowels (ü)
exercises.meaning: Phonetic distribution of Ach-Laut [x] vs Ich-Laut [ç]
exercises.affirmation: You split the two ch-sounds by vowel depth — that is native-level hearing.
exercises.explanation: German CH is conditioned by tongue position: back vowels (a, o, u) trigger the velar Ach-Laut [x], while front vowels (e, i, ä, ö, ü) trigger the palatal Ich-Laut [ç].

exercises.prompt: Apply the K → CH shift: English 'to make' → German verb:
exercises.affirmation: You heard make soften to machen — the ghost in the throat, found again.
exercises.explanation: Voiceless stop K shifted to velar fricative CH + infinitive suffix -en.

exercises.idea: you walk in on a friend cooking and ask what they're doing in the kitchen
cues: Ask with was: W-word first, verb in position 2 — was machst du
make → mach- (K → CH) + the thou-ending: machst
The kitchen carries the same shift: in der Küche
exercises.target_answer: Was machst du in der Küche
exercises.meaning: What are you doing in the kitchen?

vocab_hints.note: K → CH shift: make ↔ mach + Shakespearean -st

exercises.explanation: Question order: W-word, verb in position 2, subject, then the place — the frame you just built, from a thought.

summary.outcome: Recognize common k and ch cognates and ask a simple question about an activity.

use_example.german: Was machst du in der Küche?
use_example.english: What are you doing in the kitchen?

summary.takeaway: English 'k' after vowels systematically softens to German 'ch' ([x] after a/o/u, [ç] after e/i/ä/ö/ü).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the kitchen & book set — Küche, Buch, Milch, suchen: and the seek/beseech proof that English ran this shift too.

twist.prompt: Same question, sharper nose: what are you COOKING in the kitchen? (Same shift, different root.)
twist.target_answer: Was kochst du in der Küche
twist.explanation: machen → kochen, the same K → CH receipt: machst → kochst. The question frame doesn't move — only the root changes.

brechen.context_phrase: Ich will das Glas nicht brechen.
brechen.context_translation: I do not want to break the glass.
brechen.etymology_derivation: k → ch (Ich-Laut [ç] after front vowel e).

suchen.context_translation: I am looking for my glasses.
suchen.etymology_derivation: k → ch. Direct transitive object without prepositions.

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

küche.context_translation: We are cooking in the kitchen.

hals.context_phrase: Sie trägt einen Schal um den Hals.
hals.context_translation: She wears a scarf around her neck.
hals.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *halsaz — Old English heals was the cognate; modern English neck is unrelated. [wiktionary]

neun.context_phrase: Das Kind ist neun Jahre alt.
neun.context_translation: The child is nine years old.
neun.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *newun — the direct twin of English nine. [wiktionary]

lamm.context_translation: We are grilling lamb on Sunday.
lamm.etymology_derivation: Lamm — from Proto-Germanic *lambaz, the exact cognate of English lamb; the silent b is a shared West Germanic quirk. [wiktionary]

handtuch.context_translation: The towel is hanging in the bath.
handtuch.etymology_derivation: Attested as Old High German hanttuoh; a compound of Hand and Tuch, literally hand cloth, with Hand a direct cognate of English hand. [wiktionary]

frosch.context_translation: The frog sits by the pond.
frosch.etymology_derivation: From Old High German frosk, from Proto-Germanic *fruskaz, from PIE *prew-, to jump. Dialectal English frosh is the listed cognate, and frog is named in the Bavarian section. [wiktionary]

braut.context_phrase: Die Braut trägt ein weißes Kleid.
braut.context_translation: The bride wears a white dress.
braut.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *brūdiz, Old High German brūt, the exact twin of English bride. [wiktionary]

lügen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *leuganą; the page documents cognate English lie (the tell-a-lie one). The ü spelling was standardized to keep the word apart from liegen (to lie down). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
